title: ISO 15189 — Medical Laboratories: Requirements for Quality and Competence
shortDescription: The standard written specifically for medical/pathology labs — patient results, not just generic testing.
genZNote: Medical labs need receipts for competence, not just confidence.

sections.heading: What It Is and Who It's For
bullets: Full title: 'Medical laboratories — Requirements for quality and competence.'

Written SPECIFICALLY for medical/clinical/pathology laboratories — pathology, microbiology, biochemistry, haematology, immunology, and molecular diagnostics labs that produce results used directly in patient care.
Combines general laboratory-competence requirements (similar territory to ISO/IEC 17025) with medical-specific requirements around patient safety, sample handling, and clinical interpretation.

sections.heading: Pre-Examination, Examination, Post-Examination
bullets: Pre-examination (pre-analytical) phase — everything from the clinician's test request through patient preparation, sample collection, handling, and transport to the lab. A huge share of real-world lab errors happen here, before testing even begins.
Examination (analytical) phase — the actual testing process: methods, equipment, reagents, and the technical performance of the test itself.
Post-examination (post-analytical) phase — result review, interpretation, authorization, and reporting back to the requesting clinician, including how urgent/critical results are communicated.

sections.heading: Personnel Competence and Equipment
bullets: Requires documented evidence that laboratory personnel are competent for the specific tasks they perform — not just generally qualified, but specifically assessed on the actual test/method they run.
Requires equipment to be properly calibrated, maintained, and where relevant, its performance verified before being used for patient testing.
Requires measurement/result TRACEABILITY — the ability to link a reported result back through an unbroken chain of calibrations to a recognised reference.

sections.heading: Quality Assurance and Reporting
bullets: Internal quality control (running known controls alongside patient samples to catch problems in real time) and External Quality Assessment / Proficiency Testing (comparing the lab's results against other labs via an outside scheme) are both required elements.
Continual improvement — the lab must have a process to identify nonconformities, investigate root causes, and improve — the same principle running through every modern ISO management-system standard.
Results must be reported in a way that is clear, accurate, and includes information needed for correct clinical interpretation — not just a raw number.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: ISO 15189 sets quality and competence requirements specifically for medical laboratories, covering the pre-examination, examination, and post-examination phases of patient testing.
keyFacts: Written specifically for medical/clinical/pathology laboratories, unlike the more general ISO/IEC 17025.
Three core phases: pre-examination (pre-analytical), examination (analytical), post-examination (post-analytical).
Requires documented personnel competence for specific tasks, equipment calibration/traceability, and both internal QC and external proficiency testing.
In India, medical laboratory accreditation against ISO 15189 is carried out through NABL.
commonConfusion: ISO 15189 is specific to MEDICAL laboratories — a general testing/calibration lab (e.g. a materials-testing lab) would instead use ISO/IEC 17025.

highYieldFacts: ISO 15189's three phases: pre-examination, examination, post-examination — a frequently tested sequence.
ISO 15189 combines general lab-competence requirements with medical-specific patient-safety requirements.
In India, NABL accredits medical laboratories against ISO 15189.
commonTraps: Do not use ISO 15189 and ISO/IEC 17025 interchangeably — 15189 is medical-lab-specific; see the next topic's comparison table for the precise distinction.
Do not skip the pre-examination phase when listing ISO 15189's scope — most real-world lab errors occur here, not during testing itself.
mustRemember: 'Traceability' in ISO 15189 means linking a result back through calibrations to a recognised reference standard.
Both internal quality control AND external proficiency testing are required — one alone is not sufficient.
